en: Abhinavagupta: Mālinīślokavārttika, Second Section (Kāṇḍa)
Thus the god Maheśvara, established as the self of the universe, is worshipped through the sequential practice of knowledge and yoga, by means of meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās). // 2.1 //
In the eighteenth chapter, the reality (tattva) is correctly elucidated—that reality which has transcended the net of duality, impurity, māyā, and so forth. 2.2.

In this [state], practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) are described precisely as things to be abandoned; for they possess no utility whatsoever toward the attainment of supreme realization. (2.3)
How can that which is firmly rooted within internal consciousness be transferred externally into the body, breath, and intellect? Thus, the sequence of the yoga of practice must be accomplished;
for those who are intent on purifying this consciousness by means of the path of practice.
We are left in doubt as to what they do, where, from whence, and in what manner they act. (2.4)

For repetition (abhyāsa) means occurring again and again; and that [repetition] too, due to the distinctions of space and time, arises from the conjunction with either manifestation or its opposite, and occurs within the path of the body, mind, vital breath, and senses. // 2.5 //
Those who desire to enter the state of Bhairava, which is a single mass of light, remain perfectly established simply by resting in consciousness that is once-and-for-all manifest. (2.6)
Right hereafter, that limb which is beneficial to all is proclaimed;
for even the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) are determined by its gateway and are of that same nature. (2.7)
Now, in the absence of a firm foundation, what confidence can be placed in reasoning? Or is it that your own words are not likewise struck down by such lack of foundation? (2.8)
For how can those who have determined that scripture alone is the sole means of valid cognition reach a certainty when faced with a multitude of scriptures that contradict it? (2.9)
However, the fact that it is well-known among the great masses is not a cause for its validity there, because it is possible for a great mass of people who hold views contrary to it to exist. (2.10)
Even perception, regarding inclination and so forth, is indeed a vessel for an infinite regress of subsequent cognitions that perceive the sublation of what was previously seen. (2.11)
Since even one's own self-awareness is sublated right there, how indeed could this person—who is supposedly skilled in synthesizing distinctions—engage in worldly transaction? (2.12)
But for us, there shall never be a lack of foundation anywhere,
for whom the supreme ocean of terror is everywhere complete.
But specifically, it is with regard to those very people that reasoning is unstable—those for whom the supreme nectar of consciousness has been attained by crossing the ocean of reasoning. (2.14)
For indeed, all branches of reasoning, failing to touch upon self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), have nowhere attained the auspicious state as their ultimate fruit. (2.15)

For the entire meaning of the scriptures has non-duality as its essence; those of deluded intellect take delight in the distinctions that have been set forth therein for the sake of attaining it. (2.16)
And reasoning (*tarka*) is uniquely skilled in cutting away the arguments for the doctrine of difference; surely, even regarding non-difference, there is some utility for reasoning. (2.17)
And even that [duality] is not at all inconsistent with the vision of supreme non-duality;
for this very reason, he declares the supreme means for that supreme non-duality—which consists in the grace of the universe—to be the Heart, whose nature is vibration. (2.18)
That self-reflection within the heart, which consists of awakening, is the wonder of the full consciousness;
it forcibly and instantaneously dissolves the vibration of the universe all at once. (2.19)

That which is fully replete with the radiant bliss arising from the beginningless and endless states of grasping at existence and so forth, and which consists of the joy of the world, is called the universal vibration (sāmānyaspanda). // 2.20 //
To the extent that this palpitation of the heart—which is indeed manifest as the abode of emission—appears as "Being" (sat), to that same extent it enters here into the power of Trika. (2.21)
This very heart is defined as the supreme nectar of Bhairava-consciousness;
it, abiding in the trident of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, is then emitted into the supreme abode.
This entire universe, which is of the nature of consciousness, flashes forth within the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self;
it then proceeds through the path of emission on the plane of Śambhu, situated upon the trident of the three powers.

Thus, that which is sung as "Sat" (Being) is this very full heart, consisting of the "I-am-ness" (aham); it shines forth eternally as the very essence of the vibration arising from the union of Śiva and Śakti. // 2.24 //

Here, the sequences of creation, dissolution, and maintenance shine forth perpetually by the Eternal Self— whether by the hundreds or even by the thousands of millions— accumulated through the causes that are Hara, Viṣṇu, and the Lotus-born.
But here, for one who is unable to enter immediately through the previously mentioned collection of methods, the vibration of the Heart is revealed by way of the Śākta-upāya. (2.26)

Having gained access to the path of the heart by impelling the vital breath toward the tip of the trident, he becomes intent on resting within the digit of the moon of consciousness situated therein. // 2.27 //
Then, instantly, by abandoning that state, one casts off those five states beginning with "joyless," which are situated within the midst of the five elements. (2.28)
One should abandon the preceding [state] and leap over to the subsequent one, being intent on perfect rest,
for from that arises the ground consisting of innate bliss, which follows upon the state of peace.

The two, Nirānanda and Parānanda, are joined with the Puruṣa; they experience the expansion of bliss produced by the mass of objects of enjoyment, which are both non-different from and distinct from [the subject]. // 2.30 //
An indescribable state of great bliss, characterized by the left-hand path (vāmācārā), shall manifest within the great abode of Bhairava, wherein all consciousness is fully embraced.
Great bliss, having become the bliss of consciousness, proceeds ever more intensely within this state where the entire triad of right, left, and upward channels has been appropriated.

In the Trika, which consists of the synthesis of duality and non-duality through its entire essence, [the deities] are either non-different, or different, or even both different and non-different. (2.33)

When the states (bhāvas) are joined with the five stages beginning with one's own bliss (nijānanda), they become possessed of the exalted stage of the universal bliss of the world (jagadānanda). // 2.34 //
Intrinsic bliss (*nijānanda*) is based solely on resting in the aspect of the subject;
whereas the state consisting of the absence of bliss (*nirānandātmikā*) arises from resting in mere emptiness (*śūnyatāmātra*). (2.35)

When there is a resting upon the stages of the objects of knowledge, supreme bliss arises fully; yet when the object of knowledge is entirely filled by the convergence of an infinite multitude of objects, [that bliss is even more complete]. (2.36)
Because there is no further need for the act of savoring once the means of knowledge has been exhausted, the established state is called "Great Bliss" (mahānanda);
it is the expert who swallows the entire stream of the objects of knowledge along with the instruments of their measurement. (2.37)
When one attains a rest that is perfectly full and free from all limiting conditions, then indeed there is the bliss of consciousness, which is not augmented by anything insentient. // 2.38 //
And there is no fixed abode whatsoever that is differentiated or insentient in nature; there is no exclusion therein, for it vibrates everywhere as the universe. (2.39)
"That which is devoid of perceived consciousness and nourished by the supreme nectar—that alone our Guru has proclaimed to be the abode of the bliss of the universe. (2.40)
Where there is no primary applicability of meditative cultivation and the like, there one should find rest through the yoga of mental recitation. (2.41)
That which is perfect rest therein is called supreme non-duality, through the application of the staff of breath (prāṇadaṇḍa) by which the prior and posterior are equalized. (2.42)
The ground of the palace was sprinkled with water dripping from lotus-clusters suspended from the balconies;
there, by means of the distinction between bondage and liberation, the yogi—other than a mere human—proceeds through the activity of speech by way of the nature of the Unsurpassed (anuttara). 43.
By means of the yoga that causes the dissolution and emergence of the supreme egoity consisting of the reflective awareness of consciousness.
When the objective state has been illuminated by the Sun, who consists of twelve digits and is emptied by the power of exertion, it becomes filled and thoroughly investigated. // 2.45 //

By the power of being slowed down by that swallowing, as the [individual soul] enters the fire of consciousness while properly dissolving the sixteen constituent parts (kalās), it partakes of the state known as the sixteen-fold division.

There are four life-sustaining [energies] belonging to one whose state is unmodified by emission once it has been attained; they encompass within themselves all principles from *ka* to *kṣa*, and arise from the heart through the absence of reflective awareness regarding the essence of the existence of all things. (47)
By one who rests upon the leader of the family of those with immediate yoga, which brings forth externally.
She who is eternally established in the state of union with Rudra—her, the garland of steps of power that culminates within consciousness, vital breath, qualities, and the body; 2.49.

Then, having emitted [the breath] through the emission (*visarga*) moving within the belly, and having embraced the stage of emission which possesses the state of the "fish-belly" (*matsyodara*), // 2.50 //
Having ascended to the supreme digit (kalā), which is all-pervading, the sustainer of all life, and the source of the trident, situated at the junction of the three channels (nāḍīs). // 2.51 //
It is a series of steps for the power [of consciousness]— consisting of the brow-furrow, the point, and the end of sound— which, having been expanded and contracted, gradually attains oneness.
It was filled with the repeated contraction and expansion caused by the discharge of the female donkey and mare,
and it was overflowing with the surging mass of states of being that were repeatedly dissolved and created.
She whose abode is the emission of the great root-piercing spike unified as one, and who rests in the heart of Bhairava, which nourishes the totality of all states of being.
This [speech], which has acquired a supreme designation through its skill in fulfilling all things, is devoid of beginning and end, and is characterized by its inclination toward the entire universe.

Having attained the Goddess, who is the moonlight of the consciousness-moon in the space of the heart's awakening and who presides over the triad, what indeed does one not obtain? One obtains everything. (2.56)
Therefore, in this case, when the Supreme exists and the yogi desires to enter into it by means of the methods pertaining to the body of meditative cultivation, he first trembles. (2.57)
Having practiced for hundreds of previous births the conviction of identity with the body, he considers the oneness of consciousness and the body to be like that of water and mud. (2.58)
One should first enter the perfect conscious self, which is devoid of the illusion called duality, by means of the sequence of ascending through one's own power. (2.59)
That sleep would be one that causes the slackening of the body's possession [of consciousness], as long as the firm rooting in the Supreme Self has not yet occurred. (2.60)
This is the unmanifest sign (avyaktaliṅga), consisting of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva,
wherein this entire universe is dissolved and from which it is understood to have emerged.
Furthermore, it has already been determined that this [reality] is unborn; through its very presence within the body, immersion (samāveśa) shall attain clarity by virtue of its unfolding. (2.62)

The bliss of consciousness belonging to the reality of the mind, which possesses the state of its particular vibration, has within it the supreme essence of the potency of mantra, brought forth by the fullness of the unfolding of Śakti. (2.63)

This *liṅga*, consisting of the powers of *nara* and *śakti*, is both manifest and unmanifest; it is described in the scripture as the flower whose sap yields the fruit of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). (2.64)
That which is called the manifest sign (vyaktaliṅga), consisting solely of the individual person, is this threefold establishment of the differentiation of a single vibration. (2.65)
Those whose hearts are devoid of the knowledge of this internal sign (liṅga) worship external signs in vain; it is merely a labor, for that will not lead to any fruit. // 2.66 //
That which is manifest, known as the mark of the Self, residing in human form, exists when the external universe—composed of non-differentiation from the body—is full. (2.67)
For the yogi who is absorbed in the ground of great bliss, the primordial *liṅga* immediately comes face-to-face; therefore, it arises. (2.68)
One should always abide here in this *liṅga*, intent upon the repose of worship, for it is the heart of the Yoginīs and the temple of supreme bliss. (2.69)

In that [state], the wise cultivate an indescribable attainment of identity, which is a temple of bliss arising from the emission of the portions of the seed and the womb previously mentioned. // 2.70 //
Wherein, free from all exertion, this entire host of deities abides in the abode filled with bliss, consisting of the eternally manifest consciousness.
That manifestation of Bhairavanātha as both contraction and its opposite shines forth, even though for him there is no actual contraction or expansion.
When this entire universe is sprinkled by the stream of bliss arising from the friction of its completion, it casts off its antiquity.
In that regard, an effort toward entry must be made because it involves exertion; for why would one consider a lamp when the sun is ever-risen? // 2.73 //

Whether the yogi is established in his own self, situated on the ground of the vibration of Śiva’s consciousness, or whether he is one who delights in the multitude of external objects and the assembly of Yoginīs; (2.74)

Even in the absence of the jar, that state consisting of the manifestation of universal vibration—the Supreme Bhairava-mudrā, whose gaze is directed outward while its focal point remains within—is [to be realized]. (2.77)
That supreme Goddess Śivā rests upon that [foundation], which is fashioned by the play of her own sovereignty and consists of various purposeful actions.
Through the union with the essence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), characterized by an eager longing toward the flood of existence,
one abides having touched the power (*śakti*) that is the true ground of particularized vibration.
Empowered by this abiding power, their own mantras attain the capacity for autonomy in manifesting that [reality], even amidst various supernatural accomplishments (siddhis). (2.80)

Having attained firm establishment in the mode of activity that disregards both rejection and acquisition, it manifests through the union with all appearances as the conscious self (cidātman). // 2.81 //

Perceiving the object of perception as non-different from the wonder of consciousness, one sees that the state of being a coward— caused by the wretchedness of desiring purposeful action— is merely a condition brought about by one's own mind.
As long as one remains having abandoned [all else], one enters the stage of Śambhu;
indeed, one effortlessly enters the supreme stage of Bhairava. (2.83)
When consciousness is permeated by this [awareness], everything is perceived as being pervaded by the nature of light; for it is consciousness itself that shines forth. (2.84)
And it is not the case that what is unmanifest attains manifestation through its connection with the manifest, since this has already been explained in detail previously. (2.85)
With all mental fluctuations dissolved through the union of the Great Thousandfold World-system, his mind became filled with a massed, dense cloud of his own radiant light.
As long as one remains without thinking of anything, with a state free from the perception of distinctions clearly seen, so long indeed do the previously mentioned stages persist. (2.87)

They come face to face with that which is the sole cause for burning down the house of saṃsāra, and with that divine aggregate of faculties which remains hidden beneath the state of differentiation. (2.88)
When he remains for even a single moment with eyes closed, [his state] consisting solely of the instruments for play that nourishes his sovereignty becomes unfailing. (2.89)
The entire universe, melted by the great flames of awakening arising from that gateway, attains a state of resting within the ocean of supreme bliss. (2.90)
Resting in the drinking of that essence and satisfying the goddesses of consciousness, he soon attains freedom from the fear of death and birth. 2.91.
For when consciousness has reached a state of solidification— attaining the nature of being known through the body and senses—
it returns, by means of reasoning, to its own essence as a mass of pure consciousness, having attained a state of dissolution.

By that very same reasoning through which the emergence [of consciousness] occurs for those whose minds are captivated by external objects, that same [emergence] arises from the consciousness of Bhairava-bliss. (2.93)

By that very [means] obtained through the succession of oral instructions from the mouth of the Yoginī, one remains in a state consisting of pure consciousness, with all defilements and obsessions shaken off. // 2.94 //
When the yogi slightly opens his mouth, all the consciousnesses that reside within the channels of the senses and depend upon the traversal of the cakras are awakened. (2.95)

Then, because they are oriented toward consciousness, those [cognitions] characterized by distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth, forcibly attain an expansion consisting of the absence of distinction from the object to be grasped. (2.96)

The distinction between the grasped and the grasper is instantly shattered by that [wisdom] which has ascended to the mouth of the Yoginī and been obtained through the lineage of oral transmission. (2.97)
With his entire being sealed by the mudrā that bestows immediate experience,
he is unwearied Bhairava, the manifest embodiment of consciousness who presides over all.
Overcome with wonder, that yogi attains the self-awareness of his own nature, which remains unshakable even amidst the arising and passing away of various objects of perception. (2.99)
The water situated in a pond does not flow elsewhere, even with effort, for it is incapable of filling anything beyond its own measure. (2.100)
But when the interior is filled with the flow of water from the door through the power of *rasa*, then the streams issuing from all directions will become full. (2.101)
Thus, through the impetuosity of its own radiance, consciousness itself, unfolding spontaneously, manifests the various aspects of existence as non-different from its own self, without any division.
If the ground were to resort to the state of becoming an object of unification for even a moment through the dissolution of illusion, it would shine as the state of Bhairava. (2.103)
For differentiation is indeed optional; whatever distinction it may later reveal is itself the Māyā of the Sovereign, which manifests the perception of duality. (2.104)
For that [impurity] cannot exist rootless for one who has ascended by a mere opening of the eyes;
so what is the use of saying more? Such is the case in the system whose nature is the Unsurpassed (Anuttara). (2.105)
In reality, no limb of yoga possesses the status of a means, for its own nature is formless, being devoid of all limitations. (2.106)
Even this method is not a true method, because it does not cease the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
for this body of subtle wind is devoid of both exhalation and inhalation. (2.107)
In this way, even while the mind is sinking into the flavor of sense objects, it delivers itself from the domain of the ocean of differentiation. 2.108
Those who restrain their own path of the mind, like that of a horse, do not become internally moistened, just as a water-tight gourd does not. (2.109)
Because their minds are engaged in refuting those [teachings], they wander along millions of wrong paths; thus, their minds generally long for something else, even amidst suffering. (2.110)
One may become detached even from pleasure through knowledge, thinking "this is that"; for thus has the Guru instructed in many ways in his own teaching. (2.111)
The activities of the senses subside only through disregard and dispassion;
for as long as they are being restrained, they continue to undergo transformation.
Even this so-called withdrawal (pratyāhāra), which is practiced within the web of the senses, is a bondage as firm as adamantine cement for one whose activity is mounted upon bondage. (2.113)
With their minds submerged [in the Self], they do not enter into objects, nor into the means of enjoying them, nor into the pleasure or pain arising from them, being free from all doubt.
They know within themselves the happiness that comes from the cessation of worldly activity. // 2.114 //

While the self, which is the splendor of the nature of consciousness, exists within the mind and provides assistance to it, and while the group of sense organs, skilled in its operation, also exists, and while objects such as tastes and so forth are present, there arises that which is utterly devoid of differentiation.
The yogi remains there, adorned with full rays; let that reality be taken up.
The mere popular saying that "non-discrimination alone is the supreme [cause] here in this saṃsāra" is indeed true;
for non-discrimination alone is the supreme ladder for attaining the highest good. (2.116)
Abandon your attentions; indeed, where can you possibly fix your attention? Examine this for yourself:
it is certainly not fitting to fix one's attention upon that which is already full.
And it does not attain the state of reality unless it is complete. // 2.117 //
Wherever there may be the yoga of bliss, surely there the nature is complete.
If this delusion of duality were to cease— that is, if one were to reach the state of tranquility therein—
then the Lord of the Great Wheel of Consciousness would be present in all states, even in waking and so forth, upon the realization of that [bliss].
The yogi shall arise, blazing with the potency of mantra, even while traversing various paths of worldly activity. // 2.118 //
For just as one who intends to dig a well attains fulfillment only when water is reached,
whereas another [is satisfied] merely by water already held in his hand;
Thus, the method for attaining the supreme is manifold.
Therefore, this is a lack of means; for how else could a person be liberated from the bondage of duality through the application of both means and the goal? (2.120)
Even though this is not the actual means, because it functions as something related to the means, this instruction regarding the means has been set forth in many ways in this treatise. (2.121)
Just as children are clearly introduced to reality through the letters of a script which themselves consist of phonemes, so too are the ignorant led step by step by those skillful means. (2.122)
And for that very purpose, even regarding the non-dual supreme reality, some appropriate forms of worship, meditation, and so forth are respectfully described in this scripture. (2.123)

Whatever gladdens the mind, wherever the senses may be situated, should be joined to the abode of the True Brahman, which is Consciousness, within the nature of the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*). (2.124)
By relying on the state of immersion into the true being that follows the Self,
in the sequence of worshiping the various circles of powers of the lords of the supreme family,
one naturally attains the status of an instrument without effort. (2.125)
Having made the foundational earth purified by the sprinkling of the essence of wonder,
[he worships] with the naturally blooming flowers gathered from the mind, which abound with their own fragrance,
following the sequence of the priceless offering-vessel of his own heart, which is overflowing with the nectar of bliss.
I worship you, together with the Goddess, day and night in the temple of the body.
Thus, wherever it may abide by virtue of its own nature as self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), there the penetration of the three powers (*śaktitraya*) shines forth in a threefold manner. (2.127)
The repose occurring in a single moment of that which appears in nine ways from the aforementioned twelve wheels is the state consisting of one hundred and eight [pulses]. // 2.128 //
The number one hundred is perceived as that very state;
thus, whatever may be the statement of this yogin, [it is so]. (2.129)
That very [state] arises perpetually for the practice of recitation on the unsurpassed path, without depending at all upon the presence of internal fuel. (2.130)
If one considers the entry of all phenomena into that very place which blazes with hundreds of cresting flames extending from the entire multitude of sense-faculties; // 2.131 //

Surely, by means of the sudden and forceful incineration of their gross forms, they spontaneously attain identity with the light of the great flame of awakening in its essential nature; this is considered the supreme oblation in the Bhairava tradition. (2.132)

When phenomena are properly offered as oblations into the fire within the belly of one's own awakening through the proper method, they abandon their division into duality; for by their own power, they kindle that very [awakening]. (2.133)
Whatever object of the senses one creates before oneself by one's own will through the power of the inherent nature of creation, that indeed serves for meditation. (2.134)

For although the abode of consciousness is formless and consists of the forms of the entire universe, for those seeking a specific fruit, a particular form remains as the object of meditation. (2.135)
For just as one fetching water from a substance that is undifferentiated and complete seeks a jar—desiring it by setting aside other forms. (2.136)
In the same way, through the unfolding of the supreme Lord’s necessity (niyati), a certain form produces a specific determination of its fruit.
But for one whose mental activity is fully perfected and who desires no fruit whatsoever, meditation on the universal form unfolds at all times. (2.138)
Just as for a family yogin who is reeling from the intoxicating liquor of the overflowing essence of Bhairava, whatever arises does so in such a manner. (2.139)

In the Northern tradition, the mudrā is that which consists of the penetration into the body characterized by exhilaration and melting; it is the seal (mudrā) that has taken the world into itself. (2.140)
This particular method of yoga resides in the heart of someone or other, by whom the wheel of consciousness may swiftly become gracious for one who is not subject to further births.
Even while being watched by the world, though remaining engaged in the process of binding the body, he attains a certain consciousness in an instant once yoga has become firmly established. (2.142)
In this very matter, however, the wisdom of our former teachers strongly maintained the non-existence of the delusive manifestations of worldly existence. (2.143)
Enough with the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Bhedavāda, Nyāya, the teachings of the Sugata, worldly systems, the Pañcarātra, the treatises on ritual action, the established doctrines, and so forth. (2.144)

By all those who, through their respective application of propriety, have ascended to their own specific methods and cultivated the portions of knowledge and action that are appropriate and fitting. (2.145)
In this [work], the sequence of actions such as sowing seeds and digging was performed by Śambhu, which has become exceedingly extensive through its many branches. (2.146)

This unsurpassed fruit belongs to that tree which is the descent of the Bhairava of Consciousness; it is not attained through the practices of those established in the stages of life, nor by means of matted locks, collyrium, or the like. (2.147)
Wherein no distinction is found between what has been done and what has not been done—only in that very yoga should those resting find repose; for them, the ostentation of worldly existence ceases.
Like a mass of snow in the great heat of summer, it dissolves of its own accord;
for there is no need to further chew upon this flavorful wine of consciousness.

Great outpourings emerge whose number cannot be known, and their manifestations have already been set forth at length; however, regarding this reality of Abhinavagupta, only a few have attained certainty. (2.150)
Only the bee, not the fly, is truly connoisseur of the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower; likewise,
only the bee is the true connoisseur in the worship of Bhairava’s supreme non-duality.
No one who is deluded by the sense of duality feels attachment.
For one who is firmly established here, no purification whatsoever need be performed anywhere; for what could possibly be impure in this world that is of the nature of Bhairava? (2.152)
Furthermore, if the collection of elements is itself impure, by what means could its purity be established?
In this way, there would be an infinite regress, and likewise, mutual dependence would be rendered futile. (2.153)
When the impure is concealed, that which is called "pure" dissolves;
for it is produced by its opposite, not by its own nature, like the color blue. (2.154)
For this very reason, there is no attachment whatsoever to the grasping or the rejecting of objects,
for one's own nature is the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava.
For the state of being an enjoyer indeed arises spontaneously. (2.155)
Since everything here has been ordained by him,
everything is appropriate through this path;
why then discard this path for anything else?
Indeed, nothing whatsoever can possibly be considered logical. // 2.156 //
For instance, how could this so-called initiation, which cuts away impurities, be logically possible according to the position of those who maintain dualism? (2.157)
For instance, how could that which is called "impurity" conceal its own essential nature? Where, then, could there be an act of obscuration for the All-pervading Lord? (2.158)
Nor is light ever obscured by darkness, because the very arising of light consists in the act of destroying obscurity. (2.159)

Furthermore, it has been stated that for things possessing the property of motion, such as rays of light, an obstruction consists in being impeded; how could that apply to the omnipresent [Self], which possesses the property of non-motion? (2.160)

Alternatively, concealment by conventional reality (saṃvṛti) would consist merely in the obscuration of the object of knowledge—just as a cloth might obscure a jar—and not in the alteration of its essential nature. (2.161)
Moreover, because their nature is consciousness, the selves do not rest upon being objects of knowledge; thus, the notion of an obscuration of them is not tenable even in the case of words. (2.162)

But surely, for you, those atoms must be objects of knowledge for Īśvara; how then can they be such [pure consciousness], for that which consists of consciousness cannot be an object of knowledge, since its nature as consciousness would then be obscured? (2.163)
The word "cognizable" (*saṃvit-jñeya*) seems to remind one of its own linguistic twin, just as the sentence "my mother is barren" reminds one of itself. (2.164)
Furthermore, the omniscience of God is not thereby impaired by the fact that he knows atoms to be veiled; for there is no loss whatsoever on their part. (2.165)

Surely, when there is no obstruction for blue, there is no seeing because of an obstruction for the knower; likewise, there is no sublation [of omniscience], for the Omniscient One is not obscured by impurities. (2.166)
It is not so; for in that case, cloth and such things obstruct the rays of vision as they travel, but there is no possibility of an obstruction for the cognizer. (2.167)

And since impurity is non-pervasive yet acts as an obscuration for that which pervades, it would clearly follow that even in a jar, one would have to admit the presence of space by its very nature, lest it be non-empty. (2.168)
And since the self is the qualified agent, if impurity were to have no effect upon it, how could it be capable of obscuring it? Indeed, sir, what [else] could it be? (2.169)
For the mere existence of impurity is called its obscuration; an atom accompanied by impurity is defined as "obscured. (2.170)
Indeed, by this principle, even for those whose nature has been described as auspicious, there exists a veil, which is real merely by virtue of the presence of impurity. (2.171)

O Fire, calm yourself within your own self and abandon, for heaven’s sake, the display of your flaming tresses;

for there is as yet nothing to be consumed by you, the fire of the cosmic dissolution, since [the world] is not yet [ready] through the hundreds of terrible sparks that roar with deep rumbling and swirl from your blazing expansion.
Having pervaded the universe, this world, which is of the nature of your own light, has instantly attained dissolution.
In the city named Pravarapura, the Kashmiri Abhinavagupta composed this Vārttika on the Mālinīvijaya and other texts in former times. // 2.335 //
